documents.abstract: In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings, considered the gold standard of cancer management worldwide, moved rapidly from in-person to hybrid or virtual formats. It is known from human factors and team science research outside of surgery that the many benefits of remote collaboration may also come with hidden costs, such as disrupted patterns of collaborative behaviour, increased cognitive load, and reduced quality and consistency of collective decision-making. Pre-pandemic cancer care, too, exhibited disparities in case evaluations between MDTs1, partly due to sociocognitive factors (for example attitudes, team composition, and meeting organization). Contributing to these limitations are inefficient videoconferencing systems that hinder clear, inclusive, and synchronous communication, resulting in time lost to troubleshooting, divided attention, and technology fatigue2. The aim of this article is to introduce the scientific concept of proxemics and to propose human factor-informed ways of enhancing decision-making in hybrid MDT meetings for cancer management. In hybrid MDT meetings, some members are located in the same space (that is collocated) and others attend remotely via videoconferencing. Given the increasing complexity of cancer care, hybrid MDT meetings can afford greater flexibility of attendance and wider participation from specialists outside the bounds of a single site. They can minimize geographical barriers, linking tertiary centres with other hospitals within regional MDT meetings and beyond, enhance access to clinical trial opportunities, and potentially improve the timeliness of care delivery. However, clinicians have had to adapt workflows and behaviour to accommodate the specific challenges of hybrid meetings, including the inability to see who is speaking and hear remote team members clearly2, especially when video is disabled. The absence of visual cues can result in over-reliance on heuristics and an increase in the cognitive effort required to make sense of information that is shared. These adaptive responses to managing uncertainty come with a heightened potential for biased reasoning. Over 30 cognitive biases have been identified in the literature with regard to medical decision-making3. For instance, a clinician may use a recently discussed case as a reference point for judging the elements of a current case (availability bias) or selectively pay attention to information that confirms their own belief (confirmation bias). In medical teams, a consensus may be reached without consideration of all information, so as not to upset the status quo (groupthink). In hybrid MDT meetings, the lack of shared presence and disrupted communication may negatively impact decision quality in varied ways. For example, some remote attendees may exhibit reduced willingness to speak up when something does not seem as it should and other attendees may engage in more assertive communication, leading to team collaboration that is ‘linear and hierarchical’ instead of ‘lateral and inclusive’4. See Fig. 1 for a summary of challenges to efficient hybrid MDT meetings. Summary of challenges to efficient hybrid multidisciplinary team meetings and proposed workspace design solutions Proxemics refers to how physical space is understood and used to guide social interactions and behaviours. In clinical teamwork, proxemics has been studied in various contexts, including simulation training5 and telerobotic surgery6, highlighting the impact of reconfiguration of physical distances on cognitive, affective, and technical aspects of team collaboration, with implications for patient safety. The proxemics of hybrid MDT meetings can reduce shared presence, team cohesion, engagement, and task representation. This may result in greater decision-making and information-seeking influence exerted by collocated members7. The remote proxemics8 framework can inform the appropriate design and reorganization of spatial and technical elements of hybrid MDT meetings settings, so that they resemble face-to-face interaction environments, including hybrid MDT task representation, co-visualization of patient information, and user-centred approaches to collaboration. Technological debiasing solutions include: redesigning display arrangement and sizes with camera positioning in line with team members’ eye heights; enhancing gesture awareness and the ability to track others’ gaze and focus of attention; creating environments wherein individuals experience familiar everyday bodily, spatial, and social experiences; co-visualization of patient information and workflow that is user-centred and designed with a high degree of customizability, to enhance shared task representation (this includes members’ understanding of goals, decisional tasks, timelines, and information and resource requirements for task coordination and completion); and ensuring consistency in the quality and presentation of information available to remote and collocated attendees (that is what-you-see-is-what-I-see). Knowledge regarding the support requirements of hybrid MDT meetings and their influence on decision-making processes and outcomes is limited. Advances in multimodal analytics provide the means to objectively examine effective and ineffective remote and hybrid decision-making practices. Incorporating objective measures of gaze (for example using eye tracking), bodily orientations and gestures (for example using motion sensors), communication (for example using speech data), and cognitive load (for example via physiological sensors and surgical sabermetrics9) will allow MDT members to be studied with regard to how they interact with health information systems and collaborative technology. The data will provide objective metrics to compare in-person, hybrid, and virtual MDT meetings across regions and cancer types with respect to outcomes, illuminating the social and cognitive requirements of high-quality decision-making. Post-pandemic cancer care calls for a careful consideration of the differential requirements and affordances of virtual, hybrid, and in-person MDT meetings. The experience of virtual interactions afforded by the current generation of videoconferencing systems is still far from that of in-person interactions and may impact decision quality. To ensure high-quality outcomes, it is essential that technology and workspaces are adapted to humans, not the other way around. The main thrust Each and every aspect of our society has been changed by artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence is still a new phenomenon in Zimbabwe. The main thrust of this research was to understand the opportunities and challenges of artificial intelligence in training activities in the mining industry. This study was guided by understand training activities that can be transformed by artificial intelligence. The study determined the challenges of using artificial intelligence in training. The investigator obtained data through telephone interviews that were conducted with 10 participants from the Zimbabwe Mining Industry. The investigation employed judgemental, convenient and snowball sampling. The study found that there is low use of artificial intelligence in the training activities, but there are activities that can be undertaken by artificial intelligence that include induction, online training, and refresher courses. Expensiveness, lack of skills, loss of jobs, cultural and ethical implications were found to be challenges associated with the use of artificial intelligence in the employee appointment process. Efficiency, effectiveness, enhanced trainee experience, reduced costs and organisation brand were found to be benefits of employing artificial intelligence in training. The study recommends partnerships to be developed among mining organisations, higher and tertiary education, and technology enterprises to develop artificial intelligence software that can cost-effectively meet the needs of trainers.
